en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Monastic Rules (Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga), First Part.
1.8 Section on Combinations:
While engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?
While engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs three offenses.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is mostly visible, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika);
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is mostly decayed, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya);
if one inserts the genitals without touching them into a mouth that has been rounded [into a tube], it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
While engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs these three offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
By how many of the seven classes of offenses are they comprised? And by how many of the six origins of offenses are they originated?

They arise. Among the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), to which legal issue do they belong? Among the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*), by how many principles are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures (*vipatti*):
they may be a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), or they may be a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*).
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within three classes of offenses:

they may be comprised within the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), they may be comprised within the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), or they may be comprised within the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four types of legal issues, it is an issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
It may be by means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and acting according to what is admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*);

it may be by means of resolution face-to-face and covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*) … [and so on] … How many offenses does one commit by discharging feces, urine, or spittle into water out of disrespect?
One commits one offense by discharging feces, urine, or spittle into water out of disrespect.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa):
by reason of disrespect, one who voids excrement, urine, or spittle in water incurs this one offense.
To how many of the four failures does that offense belong? To how many of the seven classes of offenses?
By how many classes of offenses is it comprised? From how many origins of offenses among the six does it originate?
To which of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) does it belong? By how many means of settlement among the seven is it settled?
That offense belongs to one of the four failures (*vipatti*).
Failure in conduct.
It is comprised within one of the seven classes of offenses—
the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four legal issues, it is the legal issue of an offense.
Among the seven methods of settling disputes, a dispute may be settled by three methods:
it may be settled by face-to-face settlement and by acting according to what has been admitted; or it may be settled by face-to-face settlement and by covering over as with grass.
The eighth section on combinations is finished.
These eight sections have been written down by way of the method for recitation.
Its summary verse is:
"Wherein they are prescribed, and how many?"
And by way of the inclusion of failure;
by way of origin, legal issues,
and settlement, together with their compendium.
